extracted.intended_audience: international patent examiners and applicants (PCT international phase)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting, formatting and interpreting claims (and related formalities such as drawings and prohibited expressions) in international (PCT) applications, and for examiners conducting international search and preliminary examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings: formal requirements and indispensability of text matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The formal requirements relating to drawings are set down in Rules 11.10 to 11.13. Question arises whether text matter on drawings is absolutely indispensable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text on drawings (e.g., catchwords identifying functional integers like 'magnetic core store', 'speed integrator') may be regarded as indispensable if necessary to enable rapid and clear interpretation. Often such items can be replaced by a single numeral or letter explained in the description. Apply Rule 11 formalities; minimize text on drawings unless essential to interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited expressions category: contrary to morality or public order
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions contrary to morality or public order ("ordre public") should not be contained in an international application (Rule 9.1(i),(ii)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include incitement to riot or acts of disorder, incitement to criminal acts, racial/religious discriminatory propaganda, and grossly obscene matter. Rule 9 aims to prohibit matter likely to induce riot/public disorder or criminal/offensive behaviour. Invoked only in rare cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited expressions category: libelous or disparaging statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Disparaging statements that are libelous or similarly disparaging are not allowed; fair comment on obvious or recognized disadvantages (or disadvantages found by applicant) is permitted (Rule 9.1(iii)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discriminate between unlawful disparagement and permissible fair comment; fair comment is allowed when it relates to objective disadvantages relevant to invention or prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited expressions category: irrelevant matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Material that is 'obviously irrelevant or unnecessary' is prohibited under Rule 9.1(iv).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irrelevant matter includes content having no bearing on the invention or its background prior art. Matter may be obviously irrelevant in the original description or may become so during proceedings (e.g., after claim limitation). Receiving Office, ISA, Authority for supplementary search or International Bureau handle removals; applicant should be informed of category applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inviting insertion of subsequently identified prior art into statement of prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities may invite the applicant to insert references to prior art identified subsequently (e.g., by the search report) provided the amendment does not go beyond the disclosure in the international application as filed (A4.05[1]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner may invite inclusion of references and brief summaries when cited documents show stages/aspects were already known. Care must be taken not to contravene Article 34(2)(b). Do not invite insertion of treatises, textbooks, or well-known explanatory matter (A4.05[2]). Only indicate reason for inclusion unless detailed description necessary for full understanding. Lists of several references for same feature not required—refer only to most appropriate ones. Do not invite deletion of 'unnecessary matter' except when very extensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement: application must contain one or more claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The international application must contain 'one or more claims' (Article 3(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure at least one claim is present; this is a formal requirement of the international application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims: three core requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must (i) 'define the matter for which protection is sought', (ii) 'be clear and concise', and (iii) 'be fully supported by the description' (paragraph 5.02).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are central criteria used to assess claim form/content, novelty and inventive step. Examiner should check all three when searching and examining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be in terms of technical features
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be drafted in terms of the 'technical features of the invention' (Rule 6.3(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include statements about commercial advantages or other non-technical matters; statements of purpose are allowed if they assist in defining the invention. Functional limitations are acceptable where a skilled person can provide means performing the function without inventive skill or such means are fully disclosed. Evaluate functional limitations for what they fairly convey to a skilled person in context. 'Use' claims (technical application) are permissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-part (preamble/characterizing) claim form whenever appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 6.3(b) defines a two-part form 'whenever appropriate' — first part indicates designation and prior art features, second part (characterizing portion) states the technical features added to the prior art (paragraphs 5.05–5.06).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use two-part form to show which features are prior art and which are novel, but only when appropriate. If search reveals features in the second part already known in combination with first-part features, examiner may invite transferring them to the first part. If applicant chooses different but not incorrect division, examiner should generally not pursue the matter further because manner of claiming is for national laws. Invite adoption of two-part form when invention is a distinct improvement in an old combination; but where inappropriate (e.g., combinations of equal-status elements, modification of chemical process, complex interrelated systems, new chemical compounds not in a known class), other forms may be preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims may contain formulae or tables where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims, like the description, 'may contain chemical or mathematical formulae' but not drawings; any claim may contain tables 'only if the subject matter of the claim makes the use of tables desirable' (Rule 11.10(a),(b),(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tables in claims where convenient; do not object merely because tables are used if they are desirable for the subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must not rely on description or drawings except where absolutely necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must not, in respect of technical features, rely on references to the description or drawings 'except where absolutely necessary' (paragraph 5.10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use references like 'as described in part ...' or 'as illustrated in Figure 2' unless absolutely necessary (e.g., peculiar shape only illustrated, chemical products definable only by graphs/diagrams). Examiner should invite applicant to show absolute necessity before permitting such references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reference signs in claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If drawings make claims more intelligible, place appropriate reference signs in parentheses after claim features; these are aids and 'are not to be construed as limiting the scope of a claim' (paragraph 5.11).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include reference signs in both parts of two-part claims if helpful. Ensure examiners and readers treat signs as non-limiting explanatory aids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of claims: product (apparatus) and activity (process/use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two basic claim kinds: claims to a physical entity (product/apparatus) and claims to an activity (process/use). Product claims include substances/compositions and any physical entities produced by technical skill; process claims apply to activities involving the use of material products, energy, other processes or living things (paragraph 5.12).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims worded differently may fall in the same category (e.g., 'system' and 'apparatus'). Different claim categories may be included in same application if Rule 13.1 satisfied. Examiner should avoid over-rigid approach to differently worded claims of similar effect but should draw attention to unnecessary independent claim proliferation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grouping of inventions and independent claims — single inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination whether a group of inventions is so linked as to form a single general inventive concept is made without regard to whether they are claimed separately or as alternatives (Rule 13.3) (paragraph 5.14).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should object to unnecessary independent claim proliferation but may accept two or more independent claims in the same category if a unifying inventive concept exists and claims satisfy Article 6 'concise' requirement. Consider practical factors (e.g., separable sale items, different phase arrangements, multiple manufacturing processes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent and dependent claims: essentials and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications contain one or more independent main claims directed to essential features; dependent claims concern specific forms and must include all features of at least one independent claim (paragraph 5.15).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependent claims should be broad in meaning to cover more specific definitions or embodiments. Subject to Rule 13.1, reasonable number of dependent claims allowed even if features of dependent claim could be inventions themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claims must refer to and include limitations of referenced claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Any dependent claim must include a reference to the claim from which it depends and be construed as including all limitations contained in that antecedent claim (Rule 6.4(a),(c)) (paragraphs 5.16–5.17).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple dependent claims include all limitations of the particular claim in relation to which they are considered. Dependent claims should be grouped to enable association of related claims and to avoid obscurity; examiner should invite amendments if arrangement causes obscurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternatives within a claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim can contain alternatives, provided those alternatives are of a similar nature and can fairly be substituted one for another, and provided the presentation does not make the claim obscure or difficult to construe (paragraph 5.18).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure alternatives are comparable and the number/presentation does not render claim obscure. Refer to paragraphs 10.09 and 10.17 for related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-category claim references are not dependent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may refer to another claim even if not a dependent claim as defined in Rule 6.4 (for example, 'Apparatus for carrying out the process of Claim 1' or 'Process for the manufacture of the product of Claim 1') (paragraph 5.19).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such references create functional or relational links between claims of different categories but do not carry the full limitations of dependent-claim structure; handle accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation: ordinary meaning to person skilled in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be read giving the words the ordinary meaning and scope which would be attributed by a person skilled in the relevant art, unless the description gives words a special meaning by explicit definition or otherwise (Article 6, paragraph 5.20).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation for search and examination purposes should be consistent. See appendix for further guidance on interpretation. Use description-defined meanings only where clearly indicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use claims: suitability for stated use affects novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim to a substance or composition for a particular use should generally be construed as meaning a substance/composition which is in fact suitable for the stated use (paragraph 5.21).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A known product that is the same substance but in a form unsuitable for the stated use does not deprive novelty; if known product is in a form suitable for the use even if never described for that use, it deprives novelty. Claims like '... for use as a medicament' are restricted to substances packaged/presented for that use. See appendix for when 'use' claim is equivalent to 'process' claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of preamble on claim evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of the preamble on evaluation for search/examination should be determined case-by-case. Statements reciting purpose or intended use must be evaluated to determine whether they result in structural or process-step differences that limit the claim (paragraph 5.22).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In two-part claims the preamble is regarded as a limitation. Apparatus claimed 'for' a purpose means apparatus suitable for that purpose; if prior art apparatus is inherently capable of the purpose, the preamble may not limit novelty. Similarly for product-for-use claims, suitability for use is relevant to novelty evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open, closed and 'consisting essentially of' transitional phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: The type of transition phrase used (e.g., 'consisting of', 'comprising', 'consisting essentially of') determines the subject matter to be searched and scope (paragraph 5.24).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (a) 'Consisting of' generally construed as closed — excludes additional elements; (b) 'Comprising' is open — includes additional elements; (c) 'Consisting essentially of' is intermediate — limits scope to specified materials/steps 'and those that do not materially affect the basic and novel characteristic(s)'. For search/examination, absent clear indication of the 'basic and novel characteristics' in description/claims, 'consisting essentially of' will be construed as open ('comprising'). Some Authorities may vary in treating 'consisting of' vs 'consisting essentially of'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function claim interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a limitation defines a means or step in terms of function/characteristics without specifying structure/material/act, it should be construed as defining any structure/material/act capable of performing the defined function or having the defined characteristics, unless further specified (paragraph 5.25).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the means are further specified, include those further specified limitations. Issues whether such claims are clear/concise or sufficiently disclosed should be determined separately (i.e., clarity and sufficiency of disclosure are distinct assessments). Examples: 'valve means for restricting the flow of fluid' interpreted broadly to include any valve capable of restricting flow; 'layer which insulates heat' interpreted as any product layer that insulates heat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claims: product focus and novelty assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a claim defines a product by the process by which it is made, the claim as a whole is directed to a product. Such a claim lacks novelty if a prior art product, even if made by an undisclosed process, is inherently the same or indistinguishable (paragraph 5.26).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If product can only be defined by the process or process imparts distinctive characteristics, examiner should consider process steps in search and patentability assessment (paragraph 5.27). Novelty is only jeopardized if an identical product made by welding (or other process) is found in the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product and apparatus limitations in process claims must be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: Product and apparatus limitations appearing in process claims must be taken into account for search and examination purposes (paragraph 5.28).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include consideration of product/apparatus features when assessing novelty/inventive step of a process claim; see effect of preamble guidance (paragraph 5.22).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconsistency between claims and description should be remedied
rubrics_metrics.description: Where serious inconsistency exists between claims and description, amendments should be invited. Example: description implies a technical feature essential to performance but not in claims; invite amendment of claims to include feature (paragraph 5.29).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant convincingly shows description was incorrect, invite amendment of description instead. If embodiments in description/drawings fall outside claimed subject matter, invite claim or description amendment to remove inconsistency. Inconsistencies not causing doubt as to claims' meaning may be overlooked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objection to vague general statements expanding protection
rubrics_metrics.description: General statements implying protection may be expanded vaguely (e.g., to cover the 'spirit' of the invention) should be objected to as not complying with Article 6 (paragraph 5.30).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claims directed to combinations only, statements implying protection for individual features/sub-combinations should be objected to. Require precise scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity requirement for claims individually and as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be clear individually and collectively; clarity is of utmost importance for formulating opinions on novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability (Article 6, paragraphs 5.31–5.33).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms should be understandable to a person skilled in the art from the claim wording alone where possible. Analyze clarity in light of application disclosure, prior art teachings, and skilled person's interpretation at time of invention. Breadth does not equal lack of clarity. Independent claims should specify essential features needed to define the invention, except insofar as implied by generic terms (e.g., 'bicycle' implies wheels). For process claims producing a product, the process must reasonably lead to that product when carried out by a skilled person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of relative/degree terms and invitation to define
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should not use vague relative terms (e.g., 'thin', 'wide', 'strong') unless the term has a well-recognized meaning in the art; for degree terms, examiner should determine whether skilled person would be apprised of meaning by disclosure or prior art (paragraph 5.34).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If ambiguous, invite applicant to define or excise the term if possible without extending subject matter beyond filed disclosure. Applicant cannot rely on an unclear term to distinguish from prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid defining invention solely by result unless enabled
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that define invention or a feature by a result to be achieved should generally be objected to for lack of clarity, unless result-based definition is the only possible way and the description includes adequate directions enabling routine determination of required parameters without undue experimentation (paragraph 5.35).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not object if result can be achieved without undue experimentation and directions/tests are adequately specified. Example: ashtray extinguishing cigarette by shape/dimensions—relative dimensions may be defined by reference to result if description includes routine test procedures to determine required dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition by parameters acceptable only if parameters are clear and measurable
rubrics_metrics.description: A product may be defined by chemical formula, product of a process or by parameters. Definition solely by parameters is appropriate if parameters can be clearly and reliably determined via description or recognized objective procedures; non-art-recognized parameters or non-accessible measuring apparatus may be objectionable (paragraph 5.36).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: examiner should be aware applicants may use unusual parameters to disguise lack of novelty. If parameters are not standard or measurable by accessible means, object on clarity/support grounds.
